newsitem.title: FRANCE: Summary of labour unrest in France.
newsitem.headline: Summary of labour unrest in France.

text.p: The following is a summary of labour unrest that Prime Minister Alain Juppe has to contend with at a time of record unemployment and public spending restraint.
None so far has shown the momentum that produced crippling strikes in 1995. The main issues are rail reform, civil service pay and jobs, retirement, pensions, working hours and restructuring.
SNCF STATE RAILWAYS:
- January 30 one-day strike called by CGT and CFDT, first and second largest in SNCF railways, and small SUD-Rail union.
- Conflict is over reform to create state holding company to take over 134.2 billion francs of SNCF debts totalling 208 billion and become owner of rail infrastructure.
- Main SNCF unions say that under European deregulation pressures, this could threaten rail monopoly, public service and jobs. Minority unions accept reform as necessary.
- SUD Rail, strong in Paris, Lyon and some other centres, called ineffective strike on January 21.
- Rail strike in Nov/Dec 1995 spearheaded public sector strike, but government no longer planning to curb SNCF early retirement pension rights, which provoked cohesive union resistance.
OTHER PUBLIC TRANSPORT:
- Bus and urban transit staff staged one-day regional strike on January 24, called by CGT, CFDT, Force Ouvriere, CFTC, FNCR.
- Unions are seeking retirement at 55, cut in working week without loss of pay, better conditions and job creation.
- Urban transport companies are mainly private with contracts with local authorities to provide public transport
- Paris RATP public transport services suffered little from sporadic union strike calls last year.
CIVIL SERVICE/TEACHERS:
- February 1 protest rally called by FSU, the largest union among state teachers and five million central civil servants.
- January 27-31 "week of action" -- usually rallies or demonstrations -- called by CGT union.
- Main issue is pay talks after 1996 freeze for all employees in civil service, which includes teachers, health service staff and local authority employees.
- Government also plans to cut some 6,000 jobs this year, including 2,700 among teachers.
- Juppe believed ready for new pay talks, but refusing compensation for 1996 freeze. Unions want deal boosting purchasing power over 1996, 1997 and 1998.
- Second round of talks likely to start early February.

- Disputes over jobs and pay were source of October 17 public sector, nationwide demonstrations and one-day strike in rail, air, school and postal services. Civil service ministry said one in three followed the call. Unions divided.
BANKING SECTOR:
- January 28 Paris protest rally called by 46 staff unions in 14 state and semi-state bank and financial sector groups.
- Backdrop is gradual restructuring, government cuts and a banking climate which is still lacklustre. Most protests so far have been at company level and prospect of escalation limited.
- Employees of property lender Credit Foncier de France held bank chairman hostage for five days and still occupying bank to protest plan to wind it down.

- Unions are fighting cutbacks at the Bank of France and seeking moratorium on job shedding in state and semi-state institutions. Credit Lyonnais staff worried about job cuts while government forced last year to call off sale of insurer GAN banking unit CIC, in part due to worries about job losses.
- Banks are trying to negotiate deals individually on more flexible working time.
POWER UTILITIES:
- CGT says EU deregulation threat to jobs, public service.
- CGT, representing about half of staff at EdF electricity utility, also hostile to a draft agreement which would allow a reduction of the working week to 32 hours with 35 hours pay.
- CFDT, CFTC and CGC have provisionally backed deal which, if they sign up formally, would be implemented at local or plant level rather than across the board.
- Sporadic, limited protests and stoppages, no power cuts.
PENSIONS:
- Bill introducing private pension funds has provoked union condemnation on grounds it will undermine the current benefit regime funded by welfare system, discourage pay rises.
- Bill condemned by major unions due to clause exempting employers paying into funds from Social Security levies on those contributions as well as tax relief for companies and employees.

- Unions hope to use second Senate reading of bill to secure change, arguing it will drain money from existing system and prompt employers to offer staff pension funds contributions instead of pay rises, as the latter would be subject to full payroll charges.
- Unions -- the CGT, CFDT, CGC, CFTC and FSU -- refraining from predicting their response if clause not dropped.
RETIREMENT:
- Issue of early retirement reared its head after agreement by government in December to allow striking truck drivers to take early retirement at 55 after a minimum number of years' service.
- Local conflicts including protests by Bordeaux bus drivers and January 24 regional transport strike based on similar claims mixed with other conflicts over working time and conditions.

Government and opposition Socialists rule out generalised retirement at 55, government says, if anything, a strain on the pensions system will require people to work longer. National union leaders have dismissed, ducked or sidelined the issue.
DEFENCE:
- Government cutbacks and restructuring of sector have sparked sporadic protests or brief strikes by staff of state arms and defence companies or those working in naval dockyards.
AIRLINES:

- Restructuring at Air France and plans to merge it fully with its European unit Air France Europe sparked a series of one-day strikes last year, notably by pilots at Air France Europe worried about changed pay structures after the merger.
- December strike averted by setup of negotiating groups.
MAIN NATIONAL UNION CONFEDERATIONS
CFDT - Socialist. Leader Nicole Notat
CGT - Communist. hardline. Leader Louis Viannet
Force Ouvriere. hardline. Leader March Blondel
CFTC - Christian. moderate. Leader Alain Deleu
CGC - White-collar, moderate. Leader Marc Vilbenoit
FSU - Teachers/civil servants. Leader Michel Deschamps
